name: Design a Model Fine-Tuning Pipeline
intent: Let teams fine-tune a base model on their own data, prove that the result is better than what is running now, and ship it safely, without losing days of GPU work to a crash or promoting a model that only looks good.
codeTitle: a promotion gate and a run that resumes from a checkpoint
finalIntro: One fine-tuning run, from a dataset version to a canary, and a crash in the middle.
prompt: Design a platform that lets product teams fine-tune a base language model on their own data. A team points to a dataset, chooses a base model and a method, and gets back a model or adapter that is checked against the current production model and, if it is better, rolled out gradually. Runs can last from minutes to several days on a shared pool of GPUs, and the data is private to each team.
functional: Register datasets with versions, checks and a frozen test split
Start a fine-tuning run for a chosen base model, data version and settings, and follow its progress
Resume a run that was interrupted from a recent checkpoint
Evaluate every run against a frozen test set and against the model that is in production now
Record each model with the data, code, base model and settings that produced it, and promote only those that pass
Roll a promoted model out to a small share of traffic first, and roll it back quickly if it does worse
nonFunctional: A run that is preempted or crashes loses at most about 30 minutes of work
No model is promoted unless it beats the current one by a set margin and does not regress any protected slice
Every model can be traced to the exact dataset version, code commit, base model and settings
A team's data and models are visible only to that team, and a deleted record is removed from future datasets
A shared pool of GPUs serves many teams fairly, with a cost limit for each
A small run gives a first result within hours, and a large run reports its progress and expected finish time

firstAttempt.text: A script in a notebook on one GPU machine reads a spreadsheet of examples, trains, writes the weights to a folder and prints a few sample answers. The author reads the samples, decides that they look good, and copies the weights to the machine that serves the model.
limits: Nobody knows exactly which data or settings made the weights, so the result cannot be reproduced
A crash after 30 hours of training means starting from nothing
Looking at a few samples misses regressions that a test set would catch, and the same examples may be in both training and testing
One machine cannot be shared fairly, and nothing stops one team from using all of it
A bad model goes straight to every user, with no way back except copying the old weights again

steps.title: Version and validate the data
steps.problem: A model is only as good as its data, and the first script took whatever was in a spreadsheet. If the data changes, nobody can say which version a model was trained on. If the same example appears in both the training and the test split, the test score is inflated and a bad model passes.
steps.fix: Datasets are registered with an immutable version, identified by a hash of their content. On registration, checks run: schema and format, duplicates, an empty or truncated answer, personal data, and label sanity on a sample. The split into training, validation and test is made once, by hashing a stable key such as the customer or conversation id, so that related examples always land on the same side, and the test split is then frozen for every later run.
steps.tradeoff: Runs become reproducible, and leakage between training and test is much harder to cause. Registration takes time and a team must fix data problems before training, which feels slower than starting at once. A frozen test set can go out of date, so it is reviewed and versioned on purpose.

steps.title: Queue the work on a shared GPU pool
steps.problem: GPUs are expensive and scarce, and many teams want them. One machine per team wastes most of them, and a free-for-all lets one large job block everyone else.
steps.fix: A run request names a base model, a data version, a method (adapter or full tuning), the settings and the number of GPUs. It goes into a job queue. A scheduler places jobs on the pool by priority and fair share, and starts a distributed job only when all the GPUs it needs are free at once, so that half-started jobs do not hold GPUs and wait. Small adapter runs can share a node; large runs get whole nodes. Each job gets an id and a status that the team can follow.
steps.tradeoff: The pool stays busy and no team can take it all. A job may wait, so the platform shows an expected start time, and waiting is the price of sharing. Starting a job only when all its GPUs are free can leave GPUs idle for a while.

steps.title: Checkpoint and resume
steps.problem: A run may last 36 hours on many GPUs, and hardware fails and spot capacity is taken back. Without saved state, a failure at hour 30 wastes 30 hours of GPU time.
steps.fix: The job saves a checkpoint to durable storage every N minutes: the weights (or the adapter), the optimizer state, the position in the data and the random seeds. Writes are atomic: the files go to a temporary name and a small manifest is written last, so a half-written checkpoint is never used. The last few are kept. When a job is interrupted, the scheduler restarts it from the newest complete checkpoint on whatever GPUs are free.
steps.tradeoff: A failure now costs at most the work since the last checkpoint. Each checkpoint pauses training for a moment and uses storage: a full tune stores about 16 bytes per parameter for the optimizer state, an adapter run far less. Saving too often wastes time and saving too rarely loses work, so the interval is chosen from the cost of each.

steps.title: Evaluate before promoting
steps.problem: A model that looks good on a few samples can be worse overall, or worse for an important group of users. An average that goes up by a hair can be noise.
steps.fix: When a run ends, an evaluation job scores the new model and the current production model on the same frozen test set, and on named slices such as long inputs, a second language or a sensitive topic. A gate promotes a candidate only if it beats the current model by a margin larger than the noise and no protected slice drops by more than a small tolerance. Format validity, refusals and a sample reviewed by a person are checked too. The scores and the decision are stored with the run.
steps.tradeoff: Regressions are caught before users see them, and the decision is the same every time. The margin and tolerances are policy, and too strict a gate stops useful improvements while too loose a gate lets small regressions in. A frozen test set measures the past, so the rollout is still watched.

steps.title: Record lineage in a registry
steps.problem: Months later someone asks which data produced the model in production, who approved it, and how to reproduce it. A folder of weights cannot answer that.
steps.fix: A model registry stores each candidate or adapter as an immutable artifact with its lineage: dataset version, code commit, base model id, settings, the checkpoint it came from, the evaluation results and the owner. The stage of a model (candidate, approved, in production, retired) changes through the gate, never by hand, and every change is logged. Access follows the team that owns the data.
steps.tradeoff: Any model can be traced, reproduced or removed, for example when a person asks for their data to be deleted. The registry is one more system to run, and its records must be written automatically, since lineage that people maintain by hand is soon wrong.

steps.title: Roll out gradually, and be able to go back
steps.problem: A test set is not live traffic. A model that passed the gate can still do worse for real users, and a bad release should not reach all of them at once.
steps.fix: A rollout controller sends a small share of traffic to the new model while the rest stays on the old one, and compares live measures: accepted answers, complaints, latency, cost and errors. The share grows in steps if the numbers hold, and the controller returns to the old model at once if they do not. Adapters make this cheap: the same base model serves both versions, and the adapter is chosen by a flag or by customer.
steps.tradeoff: A bad model harms few users and is withdrawn in minutes. Two versions are served for a while, which costs capacity, and live comparisons need enough traffic and some patience to be meaningful.

steps.title: Control cost and access
steps.problem: A single misconfigured run can burn a week of GPU budget, and the platform now holds every team's private data.
steps.fix: Each team has a quota of GPU hours and a budget, checked when a run is submitted and while it runs. A run that stalls, with a flat or exploding loss, is stopped early and the team is told why. Datasets, checkpoints and models are encrypted and readable only by the owning team. A record that must be deleted is removed from the dataset registry, excluded from every future version, and the affected models are listed for retraining.
steps.tradeoff: Spend is predictable and a mistake is cheap. Quotas can block urgent work, so there is a way to ask for more, and early stopping occasionally ends a run that would have recovered.

failures.scenario: Test examples leaked into the training data
failures.impact: The model scores 97 percent offline, passes the gate, and does badly on real traffic. The team loses trust in the scores.
failures.answer: The split is made once from a stable key and the test set is frozen, so related examples stay together. Registration checks for near-duplicates between splits and fails the dataset if it finds them. The live canary measures what the test set cannot, and a drop between offline and live results is itself an alert.

failures.scenario: A node fails at hour 30 of a 36-hour run
failures.impact: Without a checkpoint all 30 hours of GPU time are lost, and the team's deadline is missed.
failures.answer: Checkpoints are written every 30 minutes with an atomic manifest, and the scheduler restarts the job from the newest complete one on other GPUs. At most about 30 minutes of work are redone. The platform shows the loss curve continuing across the restart, so that a bad resume is visible.

failures.scenario: A model wins on the metric and loses with real users
failures.impact: A fine-tuned model has a higher test score, but users accept fewer of its answers, because the test set does not contain the way they really write.
failures.answer: The gate is necessary, not sufficient. The canary compares live measures such as accepted answers and complaints against the old model, and rolls back on a fall. Real traffic that was reviewed is added to a new version of the test set, so the next gate is closer to reality.

failures.scenario: An adapter trained for one customer is served to another
failures.impact: Customer B's answers use customer A's tone, vocabulary and possibly memorised private text.
failures.answer: Adapters are registry artifacts owned by one team or customer, and the serving layer resolves the adapter from the authenticated tenant, never from a request field. A test asks each customer's adapter for another's known phrases, and fails if they appear. Training data is kept out of a shared base model, so that only adapters hold customer-specific behaviour.

alternatives.title: Which method to offer by default

options.name: Full fine-tuning of the base model
options.pro: Can change the model the most
options.con: Needs about 16 bytes of training state per parameter, a full copy of the model per run and long runs on many GPUs

options.name: LoRA adapters on a frozen base
options.pro: Small training state and small artifacts, many teams share one base, runs fit on one GPU
options.con: A low-rank update may not capture every change, so some tasks need more

options.name: Both, with adapters as the default
options.pro: Most teams are served cheaply, and the few who need more can ask for it
options.con: Two paths to build, test and support

alternatives.pick: Both, with adapters as the default. Most behaviour changes (style, format, a narrow skill) are well served by adapters at a fraction of the cost, and full tuning stays available behind a request for the few teams that show they need it.

alternatives.title: Where the gate runs

options.name: At the end of the training job
options.pro: Simple, and the GPUs are already allocated
options.con: Holds expensive GPUs while evaluation runs, and a bug in evaluation can fail a finished run

options.name: As a separate evaluation job after training
options.pro: Training GPUs are released at once, and evaluation can be re-run or improved without retraining
options.con: One more job to schedule and a hand-off between the two

options.name: Evaluate only in the canary on live traffic
options.con: A bad model reaches real users before anyone knows, so it is no gate at all

alternatives.pick: A separate evaluation job, then a canary. It frees the GPUs, lets the gate improve without retraining, and the canary covers what the test set cannot.

alternatives.title: Where checkpoints live

options.name: On the local disk of each training node
options.con: Lost with the node, which is exactly when a checkpoint is needed

options.name: In shared object storage
options.pro: Survives any node failure and any node can resume the run
options.con: Slower writes, so the interval and the size matter

options.name: Local first, then copied to object storage in the background
options.pro: Training barely pauses and the copy survives node loss
options.con: The newest checkpoint may not be safe yet, so the resume point can be one checkpoint older

alternatives.pick: Write to object storage with an atomic manifest for most runs, and add the local-first copy for very large checkpoints where the write time becomes expensive.

roles.label: Teams and traffic
roles.description: The product teams that submit runs, and the users whose requests a promoted model serves.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The run API and the rollout controller.

roles.label: Processing
roles.description: Validation, training, evaluation, scheduling and serving.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Datasets, checkpoints, the frozen test set, the registry and the quotas.

quiz.question: A candidate model scores 0.5 points higher overall than the production model on the frozen test set, but 3 points lower on inputs in a second language that matters to the business. What should the gate do?
options: Promote it, because the overall score is the number that the business has chosen to track
Reject it or hold it for review, because a protected slice regressed by more than the tolerance
Promote it to half of the traffic, and wait for users to complain about the second language
Average the two scores, and promote the model if the average is above the current one
quiz.explanation: An overall average can hide a loss for a group that matters. The gate checks named slices as well as the total, and a drop beyond the tolerance blocks promotion, whatever the average says. Promoting to half the traffic, or averaging the scores, lets the regression reach users.

quiz.question: A 36-hour fine-tuning run crashes at hour 30 on a shared pool. The team had no checkpoints. What is the best change to prevent this from costing 30 hours again?
options: Run the job on a single larger machine, which crashes less often than a group of machines
Shorten the run to 12 hours by using fewer examples, whatever it does to the quality
Save the weights, optimizer state and data position to object storage every 30 minutes, and resume from the newest complete one
Ask the team to watch the run and restart it by hand from the beginning when it fails
quiz.explanation: Checkpoints bound the work lost to the interval between them, and storing them off the node lets any machine resume. A bigger machine still fails, fewer examples change the model, and manual restarts from the beginning lose all the work again.

quiz.question: A model's offline score is 97 percent, and in the canary its answers are accepted much less often than the old model's. What is the most likely cause and the right response?
options: The test set does not look like live traffic, or leaked into training, so roll back and fix the evaluation data
The canary is too small to be meaningful, so ignore it and promote the model to all users
Users need time to get used to a new model, so keep it in production for a month
The model is too good, so lower its learning rate and train it again from scratch
quiz.explanation: A big gap between offline and live results means the offline numbers do not measure what users experience, for example through leakage or an unrepresentative test set. Roll back, then rebuild the test set from real traffic. Ignoring the canary or waiting hides the problem from the team.
